title: Bucephalus: Afraid of Its Shadow
description: A horse no one could ride, a boy who faces it into the sun, and a city named in mourning—Go Deep into one taming that made a conqueror.
imageHint: Dust, sun, and a horse that feared its own dark twin

questions.question: According to Plutarch, which Macedonian prince tamed a warhorse by turning its head toward the sun—away from its own shadow?
questions.explanation: The adults had given up. The boy saw what spooked the animal, bet he could ride it, and won a horse—and a legend.

questions.question: What was the name of the horse Alexander tamed that day?
questions.explanation: The name is usually glossed as "ox-head," likely from a brand. He carried Alexander from Europe into Asia.

questions.question: Bucephalus spooked at what, which Alexander removed by facing him into the sun?
questions.explanation: Turn the head toward the sun and the dark twin falls behind. A simple trick. An empire's worth of confidence.

questions.question: After that shadow trick, King Philip bought Bucephalus for about how many talents—then told Alexander to find a kingdom big enough for him?
questions.explanation: Plutarch puts the price near thirteen talents. Philip's line: look for a kingdom equal to your ambition—Macedonia is too small.

questions.question: When Bucephalus later died on campaign, Alexander named which city for him—on the far side of his empire?
questions.explanation: Near the Hydaspes in modern Pakistan, tradition says. He mourned the horse like a friend—and stamped the name into the map.

easterEgg.title: Afraid of its shadow
easterEgg.text: Plutarch says young Alexander noticed Bucephalus spooked at his own shadow, so he turned the horse's head toward the sun. He later named a city in modern Pakistan for the horse: Bucephala.
